Decomposed latents in semantic communication retain a subject's identity, yet existing designs certify protection from the \emph{appearance} of the released noise rather than from an auditable budget, and report no adversary identification bound. We develop a framework that quantifies both. The per-component $\ell_2$ sensitivity is isolated and correct quadrature bookkeeping is distinguished from looser linear practices: at a low-noise operating point, amplitude-only $\ell_1$ accounting reports $\varepsilon\approx693$ where the rigorous Gaussian tail bound gives $\approx2441$ and the quadrature account gives $2000$ (a Gaussian-proxy re-pricing of a reference operating point). Two independent guarantees are derived. A $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP account via R\'enyi and Gaussian DP audits the release; a Gaussian worst-case mutual-information bound with Fano's inequality gives an identification-error floor $\tau$ with ceiling $\tau_{\max}(K)$. Neither implies the other. Post-processing leaves both unchanged, so a public invertible shaping network cannot help Bob without helping Eve. The induced budget program has a closed-form water-filling KKT solution. On a SemanticStyleGAN calibration, $65{,}536$ prior codes fix each block's power and sensitivity and noise sweeps fix utility weights; the accounting ordering, its dependence on task--private overlap, and the failure of amplitude-only accounting are reproduced. The perceptual score and attack error remain surrogates; source statistics are a pushforward of the generator prior, not an inversion of real identities.

Semantic communications, differential privacy, R\'enyi differential privacy, Gaussian differential privacy, mutual information, Fano inequality, resource allocation, water-filling, latent representations.

\IEEEPARstart{S}{emantic} communication compresses the source to a latent representation that carries the task-relevant meaning rather than the raw waveform. When the source is a face, that representation retains identity: the encoder separates global appearance and local part codes precisely so that the image can be reconstructed or edited, and the same part codes an eavesdropper can observe from the release. A privacy mechanism that adds noise to a subset of these codes therefore has to answer two questions that are usually left implicit: what exactly is being certified, and how much legitimate distortion the certificate costs.

The scheme of~\cite{arXiv2510} perturbs a subset of semantic latent codes, then uses a discriminator to shape that perturbation. The goal is twofold: keep the released noise close to a Laplace draw, and keep the distortion semantically mild. It is a reasonable engineering trade-off. That work \emph{does} state a nominal privacy budget --- a global sensitivity $\Delta f=351.88$, with Laplace noise $\mathrm{Lap}(0,\Delta f/\varepsilon)$ calibrated for $\varepsilon\in\{1,5,\ldots,2000\}$. What is missing is not a parameter but an \emph{auditable guarantee for the noise actually released}. The discriminator learns a pattern that only approximates a Laplace draw; the published $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ value is therefore not a proof about the released mechanism, and no identification-error statement is made. This work does not replace that design. It supplies a framework to audit any such release under standard DP metrics and to check it against an identification attack. For comparison we re-price a \emph{Gaussian proxy} of its operating point (Section~\ref{sec:experiments}): how the budget should be charged if the pattern were an exact additive Gaussian mechanism. This is a statement about the accounting law, not about the pattern's true distribution.

The framework reports two complementary evaluation tools that must not be confused. The $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP system (RDP, GDP, linear tail bound) guarantees that adjacent records are indistinguishable. The Fano certificate gives an operational lower bound on an adversary's identification error, derived from second-order release statistics. One does not imply the other: a release can satisfy a DP budget yet still leak an identifiable amount, and a release can hold a Fano floor without satisfying DP. The two are reported side by side throughout.

This gap is not unique to the reference scheme. Most existing designs optimize a learned noise-shaping network against a distortion objective; they rarely state the component-wise sensitivity of the decomposed latent, fix a composition law for the private blocks, or report a DP budget and an identification-error floor jointly. The present work starts from the sensitivity and the composition law so that the two guarantees can be priced and compared on the same release.

The contributions fall into four parts. \emph{(1) Sensitivity and bookkeeping.} The component-wise $\ell_2$ sensitivity of a decomposed latent is isolated, and the three bookkeeping rules that follow separate a correct per-component quadrature account from the looser monolithic and per-component-global practices; this clarifies how a privacy budget is charged to individual semantic components. \emph{(2) Post-processing and invertible shaping.} An invertible learned shaping cannot raise the guarantee: post-processing leaves the privacy loss unchanged, so such a component is legitimate only as a keyed, key-conditional design element. This answers whether a learned invertible denoiser can improve Bob's utility without also helping Eve. The certificate below assumes $T$ invertible and known to the eavesdropper (the worst case); a Bob-secret $T$ is reported as key-conditional rather than plain $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP. \emph{(3) Identification certificate.} A Gaussian worst-case mutual-information bound combined with Fano's inequality certifies an identification-error floor for an adversary observing the release, with an explicit feasibility ceiling $\tau_{\max}(K)$. This supplies an operational attack-error lower bound in place of a marginal-distribution ``looks private'' argument. \emph{(4) Allocation law and DP audit.} The certificate's budget program is convex and admits a closed-form water-filling KKT solution with two asymptotic regimes; the same KKT analysis gives the noise profile induced by each standard accounting law, and the static-index policy is a degenerate corner of the program. The standard R\'enyi-DP to $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ conversion and the Gaussian-DP quadrature composition are derived, and the classical linear tail bound is audited against them.

\emph{Scope of the evaluation.} The sensitivity derivation, post-processing theorem, Fano certificate, KKT allocation and composition rules are mechanism-level results. They hold for any release that satisfies the model assumptions, not just for the generator used below. The quantitative calibration does rest on the released SemanticStyleGAN generator: per-block source power, sensitivity, utility weight and shaping residual are measured on real decomposed codes and generator decodes (Section~\ref{sec:latent}). Three findings are reproduced on that measured calibration --- the accounting ordering, the dependence on the task--private overlap, and the failure mode of the amplitude-only law. Two quantities remain documented surrogates. The LPIPS score is a model-based prediction on generator decodes; the identification error against the Fano floor awaits an inverted-identity corpus with labels, as recorded in Section~\ref{sec:discussion}.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section~\ref{sec:related} positions the work against semantic-privacy, DP accounting, and information-theoretic identification literature. Section~\ref{sec:setup} fixes the latent decomposition, adjacency, and notation. Section~\ref{sec:sensitivity} derives the component sensitivity and the post-processing result. Section~\ref{sec:certificate} states the Fano identification certificate. Section~\ref{sec:allocation} solves the budget allocation, and Section~\ref{sec:rdpgdp} derives the RDP/GDP composition and the linear tail audit. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} reports the anchor, image-proxy and latent-level evaluations, and Section~\ref{sec:discussion} collects the limitations and future work.

The evaluation uses three calibrations. The first is anchored to the reference backbone and exercises every accounting rule end to end; the second is built from 500 CelebAMask-HQ faces~\cite{celebamaskhq}, with per-part variance and clipped range measured on real masks; the third is a latent-level calibration on the released SemanticStyleGAN generator, where all four calibration scalars (source power, sensitivity, utility weight and shaping residual) are measured on real decomposed codes and generator decodes. On all three, the price of a certificate is governed by the task--private overlap rather than by the reported $\varepsilon$, the amplitude-only $\ell_1$ law under-reports $\varepsilon$ at the low-noise (large-$\mu$) operating point, and a static index selection certifies no identification floor. The one remaining surrogate is the identification attack error, whose measurement against the certified floor requires an inverted-identity corpus; the stated limitations in Section~\ref{sec:discussion} record this explicitly.

\emph{Semantic representations and their privacy.} A modern generative encoder splits an image into a global structure code and part-wise local codes, which is what makes controlled synthesis and editing possible~\cite{semanticstylegan}. Over a wireless link, releasing those codes is the standard semantic-communication step --- and the part codes carry the subject's identity. Two surveys map the threat models and defence techniques in this setting~\cite{semcomsurvey_won,semcomsurvey_meng}. The reference design~\cite{arXiv2510} perturbs a subset of codes with Laplace noise, calibrated to a stated global sensitivity ($\Delta f=351.88$) and nominal $\varepsilon$, then shapes the result with a learned pattern to hold down Bob's distortion. Two things remain implicit: the \emph{component-wise} sensitivity of the decomposed code, and the composition law across private blocks. Nor does the learned released noise carry an auditable DP proof. The same pattern recurs in much semantic-privacy work, where a learned noise shape is tuned against reconstruction distortion (e.g.\ LPIPS) with no identification attack or error floor evaluated. \emph{Gap:} what is missing is an auditable, block-wise account paired with an operational attack bound --- not the mere presence of an $\varepsilon$ value. This paper starts from the component sensitivity and the composition law.

\emph{Privacy accounting.} The second reference point is the DP accounting literature. The Gaussian mechanism and its classical linear composition are standard~\cite{dwork2014}. R\'enyi DP accumulates the R\'enyi divergence of the Gaussian outputs quadratically and converts to $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ with an order-optimised bound~\cite{mironov2017rdp}. Gaussian DP treats the privacy-loss random variable as Gaussian and composes its mean and variance in quadrature~\cite{dong2022gdp}. These tools were developed and systematised alongside differentially private training~\cite{abadi2016}, where the queried statistic is a monolithic model gradient. They do not transfer unchanged to a decomposed semantic latent: the sensitivity must be charged per block, the private subset is a design choice, and a learned invertible post-processing sits between the release and the receiver. The three bounds are applied per semantic component rather than to a monolithic vector, and compared on the same release. Membership inference attacks~\cite{shokri2017} ask whether a particular record contributed to the release; the identification certificate here is a different $K$-ary problem, namely which enrolled template the released code matches.

\emph{Information-theoretic privacy and identification.} Fano's inequality offers a third reference point: it converts an information bound into a lower bound on the error of a $K$-ary estimator~\cite{fano}. Information-bottleneck and privacy-funnel formulations~\cite{privacyfunnel} trade released information against task utility by optimizing an objective. This work does not optimize such a loss. It instead derives an auditable, verifiable lower bound on an adversary's identification error from second-order release statistics. The bound is stated in operational terms the system cares about: the error an adversary cannot drive below, rather than a marginal distribution that merely looks private.

\emph{Semantic latent.} A semantic encoder (here a StyleGAN generator inverted by a Semantic StyleGAN encoder~\cite{semanticstylegan}) maps an image to a latent $z\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ decomposed into $H$ semantic components

where $h$ indexes a shared (global) code or a local (part-wise) code group. For the reference backbone, $H_{\mathrm c}=28$ codes of dimension $d_h=512$, $n=14336$; our implementation groups the 13 part-wise local codes into 13 blocks of $d_h=1024$ plus 2 shared blocks of $d_h=512$ ($H=15$, $n=14336$). Grouping affects only bookkeeping; the composition formulas of Section~\ref{sec:rdpgdp} are additive per component and are unchanged by it.

Table~\ref{tab:notation} collects these symbols for reference. Throughout, $n$ denotes the total latent coordinate count and $\ln,\log_2$ denote natural and base-two logarithms; mutual information is reported in bits and the allocation program accumulates nats (Remark~\ref{rm:units}).

\emph{Private subspace.} Let $P\subseteq\{1,\dots,H\}$ be the set of \emph{declared private} components and $Q=\{1,\dots,H\}\setminus P$ its complement. $P$ is an input design decision made by the system operator, not a quantity learned or output by the allocation algorithm: it lists the semantic attributes whose inference the system promises to obstruct (identity, in the reference task). We write $z_P=(z_h)_{h\in P}$.

Every latent coordinate satisfies $z_{h,i}\in[a_h,b_h]$; without loss of generality $b_h-a_h=b-a$ for all $(h,i)$, after the $1$-Lipschitz normalisation applied by the encoder. This common-range normalization is a modeling assumption rather than a property measured on the reference encoder weights. If a real encoder leaves coordinate ranges heterogeneous, replacing the uniform $b-a$ by the measured per-coordinate range can only tighten the sensitivity when the true ranges are smaller; the uniform value is retained here so the sensitivity stays a safe upper bound, at the cost of possibly over-estimating $\Delta f_h$.

For each block $h$, the coordinate variances are uniformly bounded, $\operatorname{Var}(z_{h,i})\le g_{h,i}$ for every coordinate $i$, and the block source power satisfies $\operatorname{Tr}\Sigma_h=\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(z_{h,i})\le g_h$. No PSD ordering $\Sigma_h\preceq\operatorname{diag}(g_{h,i})$ is assumed; residual within-block and across-block correlation is charged conservatively to the block source power $g_h$, see Remark~\ref{rm:corr}. Correlated coordinates share information, which lowers the true joint mutual information; the bound used here ignores this reduction and reports a safe upper bound on the leakage. Correspondingly, the certified floor $\tau$ is a lower bound on the identification error that a tighter, joint-covariance certificate could establish: it is a safe-side certification, but it may overstate the noise cost and make the utility look pessimistic. The relaxation never weakens the privacy guarantee.

\emph{Vector-release convention.} Each block $h$ is released as a $d_h$-dimensional vector. The Gaussian worst-case mutual information uses the AM--GM (Jensen) bound $I(z_h;z_h+N_h)\le\tfrac{d_h}{2}\log(1+\operatorname{Tr}\Sigma_h/(d_h\sigma_h^2))$ (Lemma~\ref{lm:maxent}), so $g_h$ denotes the block source power $\operatorname{Tr}\Sigma_h$; the coordinate count $d_h$ enters both this leak bound and the block $\ell_2$ sensitivity $\Delta f_h=\sqrt{d_h}(b-a)$.

\emph{Adjacency and code-level change.} A record is one face image and its associated latent vector. Two records are adjacent, $D\sim D'$, if they differ in the private semantics of exactly one subject (replace-one); every other subject's code is held fixed. i.e.\ adjacency replaces the identity-bearing private semantics of one subject. This differs from classical database DP, where adjacency flips one data \emph{record}; here the unit of change is one subject's identity code inside an otherwise fixed release, and every other subject's code is held fixed. The reference latent has $H_{\mathrm c}=28$ codes of dimension $512$, grouped into the $H=15$ blocks above; a local block concatenates two such codes. The replace-one adjacency changes only the codes that carry the subject's identity; if a concatenated block contains one changed code and one unchanged code, its true $\ell_2$ sensitivity is $(b-a)\sqrt{512}$, not $(b-a)\sqrt{1024}$. The block sensitivity used below takes the conservative worst case in which every coordinate of the block changes under adjacency, $\Delta f_h=(b-a)\sqrt{d_h}$; this over-estimates the sensitivity of a partially changed block by at most $\sqrt{2}$, and the resulting privacy accounting remains an upper bound. All quantities are per-record.

The baseline scheme of~\cite{arXiv2510} instantiates $T$ as a learned, per-component shaping network trained against a discriminator, with the additional requirement that $T$ be invertible at the legitimate receiver. Two deployment cases must be distinguished. \emph{Case (i), worst case:} $T$ is invertible and known to the eavesdropper, so the adversary observes the same release $Y$ as Bob; this is the standard $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP setting and the case certified below. \emph{Case (ii), keyed receiver:} $T$ is a Bob-secret key unknown to the eavesdropper. Post-processing still cannot raise the guarantee, but any privacy statement valid only under the hidden key is \emph{key-conditional} privacy; under the Kerckhoffs principle it is \textbf{not plain $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP}, and it is reported as such.

\emph{Adversary model.} The certificate and audit below assume the adversary observes one release $Y$ per record. In Case~(i) the adversary knows $T$ and can apply $T^{-1}$; it may hold side information about the enrolled gallery, and the Fano bound remains valid for any estimator that conditions on such side information, through data processing. The account is per-record and does not compose over repeated queries to the same subject; a multi-release adversary would require the composition rules of Section~\ref{sec:rdpgdp} applied over those releases, which is outside the single-release analysis here.

The bookkeeping ratios below are stated on the original code count $H_{\mathrm c}=28$; after grouping into the $H=15$ blocks of Section~\ref{sec:setup}, the additive composition formulas of Section~\ref{sec:rdpgdp} are unchanged. Two composition concepts must be kept separate. An \emph{amplitude-sum} account charges the sum of the per-block sensitivity-to-noise ratios, $\sum_h\Delta f_h/\sigma_h$, which is an $\ell_1$ combination across blocks. A \emph{quadrature} account accumulates the squared ratios, $\sum_h(\Delta f_h/\sigma_h)^2$, which for equal noise equals one global $\ell_2$ sensitivity query; this matches the Gaussian RDP/GDP composition of Section~\ref{sec:rdpgdp}. Three bookkeeping rules follow. Rules (i) and (iii) are the loose (and, at large $\mu$, unsound) practices that this paper audits; their $5.29\times$ ratios below are the gap between incorrect and correct bookkeeping, not a gain of any noise mechanism. In all three the symbol $\varepsilon$ denotes a noise-to-sensitivity ratio; the DP parameter further requires the tail constant $c=\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}$ of \eqref{eq:tailconst}, suppressed here for a clean ratio comparison.

\item[(i)] \emph{per-component with $\ell_1$ composition:} $\varepsilon=\sum_{h}\Delta f_h/\sigma_h$, so the smallest equalising noise satisfies $\sigma\ge(b-a)\textstyle\sum_h\sqrt{d_h}/\varepsilon$; \item[(ii)] \emph{monolithic vector query:} $\sigma\ge\Delta f_{\mathrm{glob}}/\varepsilon =(b-a)\sqrt{{\textstyle\sum_h d_h}}/\varepsilon$; \item[(iii)] \emph{charging every component the global sensitivity} (the practice implied when one reported $\varepsilon$ is reused for every code): $\sigma\ge H_{\mathrm c}\,\Delta f_{\mathrm{glob}}/\varepsilon$.

For $d_h\equiv d$, the ratios are $\sigma_{\mathrm{(i)}}/\sigma_{\mathrm{(ii)}}=\sqrt{H_{\mathrm c}}$ and $\sigma_{\mathrm{(iii)}}/\sigma_{\mathrm{(i)}}=\sqrt{H_{\mathrm c}}$; the third-to-first factor is $H_{\mathrm c}$ in noise power, or $10\log_{10}H_{\mathrm c}$ decibel.

(i) is the standard Gaussian-mechanism bound applied blockwise, using $\|\Delta z_h\|_2\le(b-a)\sqrt{d_h}$ on every adjacent pair. (ii) follows from $\|\Delta z\|_2^2=\sum_h\|\Delta z_h\|_2^2 \le(b-a)^2\sum_h d_h$. (iii) substitutes $\Delta f_{\mathrm{glob}}$ for every summand in (i). For $d_h\equiv d$: $\sum_h\sqrt d=H_{\mathrm c}\sqrt d$ and $\sqrt{\sum_h d}=\sqrt{H_{\mathrm c}d}$, giving $\sigma_{\mathrm{(i)}}/\sigma_{\mathrm{(ii)}}=\sqrt{H_{\mathrm c}}$, and $\sigma_{\mathrm{(iii)}}/\sigma_{\mathrm{(i)}}= H_{\mathrm c}\sqrt{H_{\mathrm c}d}/(H_{\mathrm c}\sqrt d)=\sqrt{H_{\mathrm c}}$.

\emph{Illustrative numbers.} Take $H_{\mathrm c}=28$ codes of width $d=512$, range $b-a=1$, and a unit budget $\varepsilon=1$ with equal noise across blocks. The three rules give the required common standard deviation $\sigma_{\mathrm{(i)}}=28\sqrt{512}\approx634$, $\sigma_{\mathrm{(ii)}}=\sqrt{28\cdot512}\approx120$, and $\sigma_{\mathrm{(iii)}}=28\sqrt{28\cdot512}\approx3352$. The gap between (i) and (ii) is purely a composition choice: rule (i) adds the 28 block amplitudes linearly, $\sum_h\sqrt d=28\sqrt d$, whereas rule (ii) combines the block sensitivities in quadrature, $\sqrt{\sum_h d}=\sqrt{28d}$; the square-root of a sum is smaller than the sum of square roots, which is why (i) demands about $5.29\times$ more noise amplitude than (ii). Rule (iii) asks for another $5.29\times$ on top of (i), and $28\times$ (14.5\,dB) the noise power of (i). Rule (ii) already matches the correct quadrature account.

\textbf{The gain exposed by Proposition~\ref{pr:inflation} is a correction of bookkeeping, not a new noise mechanism: a correct monolithic vector account (ii) is as tight as correct per-component quadrature accounting (Proposition~\ref{pr:quadrature}). Any larger privacy--utility dividend must come from the allocation itself (Section~\ref{sec:allocation}), which is a separate degree of freedom.}
Fix the noise law in \eqref{eq:mechanism}.

\item[(i)] For every $T$ that is a (possibly randomised) function of the mechanism output with randomness independent of $D$, $T\circ Y$ is $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP whenever $Y$ is. \item[(ii)] If $T$ is invertible and $T^{-1}$ is available to the adversary, $T\circ Y$ provides exactly the same guarantee as $Y$: the adversary recovers $Y$ and the protection, if any, is due to $N$ alone. \item[(iii)] If $T$ depends on the private latent directly rather than on the release, it is part of the mechanism and its sensitivity must be re-accounted; $T$ may then \emph{increase} $\varepsilon$.

(i) is the post-processing inequality: for adjacent $D\sim D'$ there is a coupling $(Y,Y')$ of the two output laws with $\Pr[Y\neq Y']\le\delta$; applying the same $T$ to both sides preserves $\{T(Y)=T(Y')\}\supseteq\{Y=Y'\}$, hence $\Pr[T(Y)\neq T(Y')]\le\delta$, and on the complement the two conditional laws coincide, which is exactly $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP. (ii) Eve computes $T^{-1}$, so the information available to her is the $\sigma$-field generated by $Y$; by the data-processing inequality $I(z;T^{-1}(T(Y)))=I(z;Y)$ and every distinguishing advantage is unchanged. (iii) $T(z+\cdot)$ is a function of the data, so the pair $(z,T(z+N))$ is released by a mechanism whose sensitivity is governed by $\|T(z)-T(z')\|$, not by $\Delta f$. A per-image contrast normalisation $\sigma\mapsto\sigma/\widehat{s}(z)$ is an instance: the released scale factor $1/\widehat{s}(z)$ is computed from the record, so it leaks through $\widehat{s}(z)$. If $\widehat{s}(z)\in[s_{\min},s_{\max}]$ with $s_{\min}>0$, its scalar sensitivity is $|1/\widehat{s}(z)-1/\widehat{s}(z')|\le |\widehat{s}(z)-\widehat{s}(z')|/ s_{\min}^{2}$; this quantity must be added to $\Delta f_h$ and re-accounted, and the normalisation cannot be treated as a fixed, privacy-neutral constant. If $s_{\min}=0$, the gain $1/\widehat{s}(z)$ is unbounded and no finite DP guarantee holds for that release.

\emph{How to re-account such a scaling.} If a record-dependent gain $g(z)=1/\widehat{s}(z)$ is released alongside the block, it is treated as an additional scalar output with sensitivity $\Delta g=|\widehat{s}(z)-\widehat{s}(z')|/s_{\min}^{2}$; this $\Delta g$ is combined with the block sensitivity $\Delta f_h$ under the chosen composition rule (linearly for the amplitude-sum account, in quadrature for the RDP/GDP account), and the allocation is re-solved with the enlarged sensitivity. The mechanism and calibration in this paper use a record-independent per-block standard deviation $\sigma_h$; no per-image contrast or gain normalization is applied, so this extra sensitivity term is zero throughout the evaluation.

Part~(ii) has a direct operational consequence: a learned invertible network cannot denoise a differentially private release for Bob alone. If Bob's decoder removes the residual noise well enough to recover a useful signal, the same invertible map applied by Eve recovers the same residual; Bob's advantage over Eve cannot come from denoising a DP release. The only way to evade this conclusion is a shaping $T$ that Eve does not know, and that key-conditional design is not standard $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP. The remaining origin of a legitimate advantage is noise whose projection onto the task subspace vanishes, which is the allocation problem of Section~\ref{sec:allocation}.

Part~(ii) imposes a constraint that applies to any deployment: DP noise cannot be ``learned away'' for the legitimate receiver only. The deprotection network at Bob is a decoder of the released signal; if it recovers $z$ up to a residual that is useful to Bob, the same architecture applied by Eve recovers the same residual. Hence Bob's advantage over Eve cannot originate in denoising a differentially private release. It can only originate in (a) a \emph{secret} shaping $T$ that Eve does not know, in which case the guarantee is key-conditional and must be stated as such; it is not $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP in the Kerckhoffs sense; or (b) noise whose projection onto the task subspace is zero, in which case Bob needs no denoiser and the protocol reduces to an allocation over the components that actually project onto the task subspace. The reference scheme~\cite{arXiv2510} relies on a learned noise pattern to keep Bob's distortion low at large $\varepsilon$. Under Theorem~\ref{th:postproc} and this remark, if the pattern is public its privacy contribution can only come from the added noise itself; a low-distortion release attributed to a public learned denoiser should be re-accounted under the noise alone, and a Bob-secret pattern should be reported explicitly as key-conditional rather than as plain $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP.

Data processing bounds the leakage of any decision Eve runs on the release. This bound converts a privacy budget into an operational error bound for the attack family the system cares about: identification among $K$ enrolled templates.

Let $\lambda_i\ge0$ be the eigenvalues of $A=\Sigma_h/\sigma_h^{2}$. By the arithmetic--geometric mean inequality, $\det(I+A)=\prod_{i=1}^{d_h}(1+\lambda_i) \le\big(\tfrac{1}{d_h}\sum_{i=1}^{d_h}(1+\lambda_i)\big)^{d_h} =\big(1+\tfrac{1}{d_h}\operatorname{Tr}A\big)^{d_h}$, which yields the second inequality in \eqref{eq:maxent}. (The commonly quoted $\det(I+A)\le1+\operatorname{Tr}A$ is \emph{false} for $d_h>1$: for $A=I_2$, $\det(I+A)=4>3=1+\operatorname{Tr}A$; in fact $\det(I+A)\ge1+\operatorname{Tr}A$, so $1+\operatorname{Tr}A$ cannot serve as an upper bound.) The AM--GM bound is tight exactly when all $\lambda_i$ are equal (isotropic block); it loosens as the source power concentrates on fewer coordinates, since that lowers $\det(I+A)$ at fixed trace.

is the largest leakage consistent with a floor $\tau$. Here $I_{\max}$ is in bits ($\log_2$); the allocation program below accumulates mutual information in nats ($\ln$), so the budget must be converted by $B=I_{\max}\ln2$ before the KKT solve (Remark~\ref{rm:units}). If $I_{\mathrm{leak}}(\sigma)\le I_{\max}(\tau)$, then \emph{every} estimator $\widehat B(Y)$ has identification error $\Pr[\widehat B\neq B]\ge\tau$. This is an operational attack-error lower bound; it is reported in parallel with the $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ account of Section~\ref{sec:rdpgdp}, and the two do not imply one another (Remark~\ref{rm:twosystems}). The feasible floors satisfy $\tau<\tau_{\max}(K)=(\log_2K-1)/\log_2(K-1)$. The source statistics are exact prior statistics: $65{,}536$ $w$-codes drawn from the latent prior are propagated through the real mapping network, giving the per-block source power $g_h$ and the 0.5\ this is a pushforward of the generator prior, not an inversion of real identities. The utility weights are measured by a per-block noise sweep: for each block $h$ and each $\sigma_h^2$ on a six-level grid, noise is added to $N=16$ codes in block $h$ only, the generator decodes back to images, and LPIPS~\cite{lpips} against the clean decode is fitted to $\mathrm{LPIPS}\approx\mathrm{lpips}_0+w_h\sigma_h^2$. The residual fraction $\kappa_h$ is the fitted residual slope of a per-block linear-MMSE (Wiener) deprotector whose covariance is measured on the same $65{,}536$ codes; the empirical residual on 1024 held-out codes matches the analytic Wiener prediction to three decimals. All runs execute on CPU, with the generator's fused CUDA operators falling back to their native CPU kernels.

\emph{Findings.} Three observations survive the move from proxy to measurement. First, the measured utility weights are concentrated: $w_h$ is large on shared\_1 ($0.342$), hair ($0.275$), shared\_0 ($0.271$), skin ($0.174$) and background ($0.170$), while the facial-feature blocks are nearly free to protect ($w_{\mathrm{eyes}}{=}0.0097$, $w_{\mathrm{nose}}{=}0.0088$, $w_{\mathrm{ear\_r}}{=}0.0078$). Visual inspection of the sweep grids shows why: the generator absorbs local latent noise into plausible variations, such as make-up-like changes around the eyes at $\sigma_h{=}0.8$ or recolouring for hair, rather than perceptual distortion, so a decomposed latent is not uniformly sensitive to noise. Second, identity is entangled with utility through the shared and skin blocks, which is what keeps the decoupled-scenario overlap at $0.590$; the certificate price is again governed by overlap, not by $\varepsilon$. Third, the audit ordering of Proposition~\ref{pr:quadrature} reproduces on the measured scalars: at quadrature $\varepsilon{=}2000$, $\delta{=}10^{-5}$, the reconstruction scenario ($\bar\mu_h\approx14.5$) reports amplitude-only $1055.2$ $< $quadrature $2000$ $<$ RDP $2037.8$ $<$ exact tail $2803.0$, and the decoupled scenario ($\bar\mu_h\approx21.2$) reports $718.4 < 2000 < 2037.8 < 2466.3$.

\emph{What remains pending.} The attack error $P_e$ is still the Fano-floor certificate evaluated against a surrogate adversary. Measuring it would require inverting a labelled identity corpus through the generator --- CelebAMask-HQ file names joined back to the CelebA identity list --- and training a recognition head on held-out identities. That is a GPU-scale inversion workload, which this CPU-only build does not attempt. The codes sampled from the generator carry no real identity, so the released calibration data raises no subject-privacy concern.
The study carries six limitations. L1 and L6 are inherent to the certificate framework; L2--L5 are limitations of the current implementation and calibration.

\item[(L1)] \emph{Attack scope (framework-inherent).} The certificate of Theorem~\ref{th:certificate} is an identification guarantee, not a guarantee on arbitrary attribute inference. It constrains every estimator of the template $B$ but says nothing about an attribute that is not a function of $z_P$. \item[(L2)] \emph{Surrogate attack error and prior-pushforward calibration (implementation-level).} The four calibration scalars are measured on the released generator (Section~\ref{sec:latent}), but the identification error $P_e$ is still a surrogate evaluated against the Fano floor, not a trained recognition head on held-out identities. In addition, the measured source statistics come from prior codes pushed through the real mapping network, not from codes inverted from real identities; an inversion-based calibration could shift $g_h$ and $\Delta f_h$ if real codes lie off the prior manifold. \item[(L3)] \emph{Manual private partition (implementation-level).} The private subspace $P$ is declared by the operator before the noise is drawn. The method does not address automatic learning or partitioning of the private semantic components. \item[(L4)] \emph{Conservative correlation bound (implementation-level).} The block-wise second-order structure of Assumption~\ref{as:indep} ignores residual within- and across-block correlation; the AM--GM second-order bound is a safe upper bound but makes the estimated utility performance look pessimistic (Remark~\ref{rm:corr}). \item[(L5)] \emph{Key-conditional mode (implementation-level).} When the shaping $T$ is a Bob-secret key unknown to the eavesdropper, the resulting guarantee is key-conditional privacy, not plain $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP under the Kerckhoffs assumption (Remark~\ref{rm:tension}). \item[(L6)] \emph{Finite template bank (framework-inherent).} For any finite $K$, the feasibility ceiling $\tau_{\max}(K)<1$; an arbitrarily strong certified identification error upper bound is unattainable, because the template entropy itself is the budget currency.
Four directions follow directly from these limitations.

\item[(F1)] \emph{Measured identification error on inverted identities.} Two of the three latent-level validation stages are complete (Section~\ref{sec:latent}): the released SemanticStyleGAN generator fixes the real per-block variance, clipped range, utility weights and Wiener residuals, and checks Assumptions~\ref{as:range}--\ref{as:indep} on the true latent geometry. The attack stage remains. Invert a labelled identity corpus (CelebAMask-HQ file names joined to the CelebA identity list) through the generator, train a recognition head on held-out identities, and measure the identification error against the certified floor, replacing the surrogate $P_e$ used here. This would also upgrade the source statistics from a prior pushforward to an inversion-based calibration. \item[(F2)] \emph{Automatic private-partition learning.} Develop a method that derives the private set $P$ from an explicit privacy target and the measured task--private overlap, instead of declaring it by hand. \item[(F3)] \emph{Accounting beyond Gaussian noise.} Extend the auditable composition and certificate to non-Gaussian noise mechanisms, where the privacy-loss distribution is not exactly Gaussian and GDP quadrature no longer applies. \item[(F4)] \emph{Tightening the correlated-source bound.} Under strong between-block correlation, estimate the joint covariance and replace the block-wise AM--GM relaxation by the exact determinant bound of Lemma~\ref{lm:maxent}, so the certified leakage reflects the true joint mutual information more tightly. \item[(F5)] \emph{Cross-release composition.} Study budget composition over multiple releases to the same subject; the present analysis is single-release and does not cover a repeated-query adversary.

Three practical conclusions follow from this study. First, the privacy of a semantic link cannot be judged from the appearance of the released noise; an auditable budget must be computed from the component sensitivity and the composition law, and reported alongside an adversary identification bound (the two guarantees are independent). Second, amplitude-only $\ell_1$ accounting inherits the Laplace-mechanism form and under-reports the leakage of a Gaussian release in the low-noise (large-$\mu$) regime, presenting a tighter-looking assessment than the mechanism guarantees. Third, a dynamic, globally coordinated budget allocation outperforms protecting a fixed subset of components: the static rule leaves the untouched private blocks released clean and certifies no identification floor. The framework is a mechanism-level, general-purpose tool for auditing latent releases that satisfy the stated model assumptions, and is not tied to SemanticStyleGAN; that generator serves only as the testbed for the numerical calibration.

The evidence now includes a latent-level measurement on the released SemanticStyleGAN generator. All four calibration scalars are measured on real decomposed codes and generator decodes. Three results reproduce on that measured calibration: the accounting ordering, the overlap--price relation, and the static-rule failure. One surrogate remains --- the identification attack error. Measuring it on an inverted-identity corpus is the first item of future work.
